{"id": "27:25/q07", "question": "What does prostration mean and why is it urged here?", "turns_on": "Whether sujūd is explained as bodily worship in opposition to sun worship or as inward actualization.", "positions": [{"id": "27:25/q07/p1", "position": "Literal worship and submission to God alone, the proper response to His power and knowledge.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī defines sujūd as placing the forehead on the ground. Ibn Kathīr says Satan kept them from worshipping God rather than created stars, citing 41:37. Al-Biqāʿī calls prostration the greatest act of nearness, prayer's restraint of wrongdoing, and the remedy to their lack of guidance. Al-Rāzī contrasts God's universal power and knowledge with the finite sun's inability to bring hidden things forth, know secrets, confer benefits or avert harm, citing 27:24 and 19:42. Al-Bayḍāwī says only the Necessary Existent can create from possibility and nonexistence. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ adds that God created even the sun and governs it while it is unaware of worshippers. Al-Ṭabrisī objects to al-Jubbāʾī that the hoopoe's distinction of right and wrong worship implies knowledge of God and divine justice."}, {"id": "27:25/q07/p2", "position": "In an inward reading, prostration is submission that brings latent perfections into actuality in the intellect.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says Satan's obstruction prevents this inner realization."}]}
{"id": "27:25/q08", "question": "Does this verse call for prostration of recitation?", "turns_on": "Whether the doubled wording's censure has the force of a command, whether the light wording is divine speech, and what the Sunnah establishes.", "positions": [{"id": "27:25/q08/p1", "position": "The light imperative calls for it, while the doubled narrative reading does not.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj, al-Qurṭubī and reports in other sources distinguish a direct order from a narrative description of refusal; Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites al-Kisāʾī's prophetic report identifying this location as a prostration place. Al-Bayḍāwī says both readings imply prostration generally but not necessarily upon recitation."}, {"id": "27:25/q08/p2", "position": "Both readings require prostration: one commands it and the other censures its omission.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī rejects al-Farrāʾ and compares the censure in 25:60. Al-Nasafī rejects al-Zajjāj on the same ground, as does al-Zamakhsharī as quoted by al-Samīn. Bursawī says the censure explains prostration at the end of these verses."}, {"id": "27:25/q08/p3", "position": "Prostration here is recommended rather than obligatory.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn appeals to the Sunnah and says a divine command would imply obligation absent contrary evidence, whereas a hoopoe's command has uncertain authority; the hoopoe seems the speaker to him."}]}
{"id": "27:25/q09", "question": "What does ٱلْخَبْءَ mean as an Arabic word?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:25/q09/p1", "position": "A concealed or unseen thing, named from the verbal noun for concealing.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba derives it from khabaʾtu al-shayʾ; al-Māwardī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn say the verbal noun names the concealed passive object. Yaḥyā notes its singular form. Al-Zajjāj says anything hidden is khabʾ; al-Wāḥidī adds stored for future need. Al-Ṭabrisī describes concealment behind a barrier preventing perception, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ transmits this. Al-Bayḍāwī describes what is inside another. Bursawī says stored and concealed; al-Biqāʿī includes actual underground concealment and potential, not-yet-existent things. Al-Samīn compares conventionally unhamzated khābiya, bariyya and dhurriyya."}]}
{"id": "27:25/q10", "question": "What hidden thing does God bring forth?", "turns_on": "Whether khabʾ is unrestricted, exemplified by rain and growth, narrowed to one material thing, or extended to creation and inward potential; the following knowledge clause favors the general sense for some.", "positions": [{"id": "27:25/q10/p1", "position": "Every concealed or unseen thing in heaven and earth.", "reasons": "Qatāda, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Ibn ʿAbbās are transmitted with secret, unseen or everything concealed; a report from Ḥakīm ibn Jābir says God knows every hidden thing. Al-Zajjāj prefers this general sense because the next knowledge clause supports it; al-Ālūsī also prefers it. Al-Ṭabrisī includes whatever perception cannot reach; al-Ṭabarī includes rain and vegetation as examples. Al-Burhān says the general wording also embraces the dead emerging alive in 99:2 and hadith treasures and minerals. Study Quran reports mysteries generally. Ibn Kathīr transmits Ibn ʿAbbās through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa, with ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Qatāda, for everything hidden."}, {"id": "27:25/q10/p2", "position": "Rain from heaven and vegetation, fruits, treasures or water from earth.", "reasons": "The common Arabic saying and many exegetes identify paired heavenly rain and earthly plants. Ibn Zayd describes provision after sky and earth were opened so rain and growth could emerge; al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Abī Ḥātim report him. Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds earthly treasures; al-Bayḍāwī adds stars and broader creation; Bursawī adds snow and water. Islāḥī includes sun, moon, Venus and Mercury above, and seas and springs below. Study Quran separately reports fruits. Al-Baghawī calls this the majority exegetical view. Al-Samīn reports the exegetical rain and vegetation gloss."}, {"id": "27:25/q10/p3", "position": "Rain or water itself is the hidden thing.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and Muqātil identify rain; Ḥakīm ibn Jābir is also transmitted with rain, despite another report about all hidden things. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib says water. The variation between rain and water is noted; this position does not specify a matching earthly plant."}, {"id": "27:25/q10/p4", "position": "Seed descends from heaven and emerges from earth.", "reasons": "Kaʿb gives this report, and Ibn ʿAbbās, who asked him about it, affirms it."}, {"id": "27:25/q10/p5", "position": "God's creation emerging from nonexistence or potentiality is likened to a hidden thing brought forth.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī treats creation from nothing as like a concealed object; al-Bayḍāwī lists creation made actual from potential and origination from possibility and nonexistence. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ makes the bringing out a metaphor for creating from nonexistence and compares the title Originator of heaven and earth; he allows literal extraction but says the place of hiding would need explanation. Al-Biqāʿī includes what does not yet exist potentially."}, {"id": "27:25/q10/p6", "position": "The sun emerges after setting, while earth brings out sperm and its formed embryo.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī ties the sun's emergence to God's control and names sperm from loins and ribs and the resulting embryo; he compares 2:258, 6:76 and 26:28. Asad connects hidden and manifest phenomena to the appearing and disappearing sun and other celestial bodies worshipped by ancient Semites, citing 6:74."}, {"id": "27:25/q10/p7", "position": "In an inward reading, it is possible perfection hidden in the heavens of spirits and earth of the body.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī relates the hidden treasure to possible human perfections."}]}
{"id": "27:25/q11", "question": "How is ٱلْخَبْءَ pronounced and explained in variant readings?", "turns_on": "Whether the hamza is kept, its vowel transferred before deletion, or replaced by alif; the dispute cites dialect, connected versus pausal usage, and transmitted recitation.", "positions": [{"id": "27:25/q11/p1", "position": "The majority keep a still bāʾ and the hamza.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān give the majority form. Al-Naḥḥās describes the still hamza at pause, possible ḍamma or imāla in the nominative, and rules out gemination. Al-Nashr calls vowel transfer at pause the standard regular treatment; Qiraat-ER describes the pausal sukūn and consonantal skeleton."}, {"id": "27:25/q11/p2", "position": "Ubayy and ʿĪsā transfer the hamza's vowel to bāʾ and omit hamza, yielding al-khab.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn report this, comparing raʾaytu al-ab. Sībawayh records such transfer for some Tamīm and Asad speakers; al-Naḥḥās quotes broader dialectal hamza substitution after sukūn, with forms al-khabu, al-khabi and al-khaba."}, {"id": "27:25/q11/p3", "position": "ʿIkrima and others read al-khabā with alif in place of the hamza.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it shortened alif; Abū Ḥayyān associates ʿIkrima, ʿAbd Allāh and Mālik ibn Dīnār and balances dialectal change against carrying a pause form into connected speech. Al-Samīn instead favors a shifted vowel with retained hamza, comparing al-marʾa and al-kamʾa. Al-Naḥḥās rebuts Abū Ḥātim using Sībawayh's account of replacement by alif, wāw or yāʾ according to vowel. Abū Ḥātim calls al-khabā non-Arabic, arguing deletion would yield al-khab and replacement al-khabī; al-Mubarrad's criticism of his grammar is reported. Al-Nashr reports Abū al-ʿAlāʾ's possible explanation by vowel assimilation at pause."}, {"id": "27:25/q11/p4", "position": "At pause, regular hamza easing allows transfer and specified assimilations, while arbitrary deletion and weakly transmitted forms are unsound.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī gives transfer as standard after a sound consonant; for kasra hamza rawm is possible, as with milʾ, difʾ and yanzur al-marʾ. After original long vowels he allows transfer or idghām for open hamza; kasra adds rawm, and ḍamma adds ishmām for six forms. He rejects al-Hudhalī's idghām for juzʾ as untransmitted from Ḥamza, and rejects arbitrary deletion, extended preceding vowels, and Ibn Ghalbūn's bayna bayn."}]}

{"id": "27:25/q13", "question": "How is ٱلَّذِى construed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:25/q13/p1", "position": "It may be genitive as adjective, apposition or explanatory substitute for God; accusative as praise; or nominative after an omitted subject.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn lists these case possibilities without preferring one."}]}
{"id": "27:25/q14", "question": "Why describe God as bringing forth hidden things here?", "turns_on": "Whether the choice is explained by a special trait of the hoopoe or by the story's disclosure and the contrast with sun worship.", "positions": [{"id": "27:25/q14/p1", "position": "It suits the hoopoe's knowledge of hidden water and its way of speaking.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says God taught the hoopoe to detect water; a report says each servant is clothed with the mantle of his work. Ibn Kathīr cites Ibn ʿAbbās and others that the hoopoe sees water deep underground. Al-Ālūsī reports the proposed connection but rejects it for lack of a reliable report and because it fails on the light reading as divine or Solomonic speech."}, {"id": "27:25/q14/p2", "position": "The attribute fits the disclosure of Bilqis and her affairs, and names God's power over the visible and hidden world.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī relates revelation of hidden realities to the narrative discovery; al-Biqāʿī says heaven and earth are the limits of human observation and lists clouds, rain, plants, celestial bodies, weather, motion and rest. Al-Ālūsī says God brings hidden states to light for recompense; al-Rāzī says the verse moves from power to knowledge. Al-Rāzī also says the order differs from Abraham's and Moses' arguments because the debate concerns sun worship; setting and rising show the sun under a ruler, citing 2:258, 6:76 and 26:28."}]}
{"id": "27:25/q15", "question": "How are the verbs for concealing and declaring read?", "turns_on": "Whether the narration stays with the absent Sheban people or shifts into direct address after the imperative or by rhetorical turn.", "positions": [{"id": "27:25/q15/p1", "position": "Both are read in the third person, 'they conceal and declare.'", "reasons": "Most readers, including Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim and the Ḥaramī readers, retain the surrounding third-person account of the queen and her people; al-Wāḥidī says Abū Bakr's version fits his recitation better than Ḥafṣ's. Ibn ʿAṭiyya connects it to the hoopoe's speech. Al-Ṭabrisī and Qiraat-ER say it avoids a shift in grammatical person; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ favors the majority reading."}, {"id": "27:25/q15/p2", "position": "Both are read in the second person, 'you conceal and declare.'", "reasons": "Al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read tāʾ in both. For al-Kisāʾī this follows the light imperative; for Ḥafṣ it may be a shift to the current audience or iltifāt. Al-Fārisī says even after third-person yasjudū it can address believers and unbelievers. Ibn ʿAṭiyya connects it to God's address to Muḥammad's community; Abū Ḥayyān offers Solomon and attendants. Ubayy's variant also uses direct address and calls the concealed one's secret."}]}
{"id": "27:25/q16", "question": "Whose concealment and disclosure does the final clause describe?", "turns_on": "The third-person versus second-person recitation and the identity of the intervening speaker.", "positions": [{"id": "27:25/q16/p1", "position": "The people whose deeds Satan adorned, the queen and her people.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī connects the third-person reading with those creatures; Abū Ḥayyān names the queen and her people. Their secret and public actions remain known to God."}, {"id": "27:25/q16/p2", "position": "The people directly ordered to prostrate are addressed.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī gives this for the light reading; al-Wāḥidī says the command continues 'who knows what you conceal'; Abū Ḥayyān offers Solomon and attendants and others take Muḥammad's community. Ubayy's reading uses 'your secret.'"}]}
{"id": "27:25/q17", "question": "What do concealing and declaring include?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause is explained through ordinary human secrets and public conduct or inward potential and moral states.", "positions": [{"id": "27:25/q17/p1", "position": "God knows every private and public word, act and state.", "reasons": "Muqātil says hearts versus tongues, as does al-Wāḥidī; Yaḥyā says breasts. Ibn ʿAbbās says night and day, and al-Ḥasan adds dark night and inside homes. Ibn Kathīr includes words and deeds and cites 13:10. Bursawī adds limbs and a Persian couplet in which not a grain escapes knowledge. Al-Ṭabrisī calls it secret and public. Al-Ālūsī says hidden states are exposed for requital and mentioning open conduct stresses equal divine knowledge. Al-Biqāʿī says even noisy, overlapping public speech is known. Islāḥī includes this knowledge in the divine insertion."}, {"id": "27:25/q17/p2", "position": "In an inward reading, God knows latent perfections and the dark dispositions or harmful morals people display.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says veiling actions block possible perfections from the intellect, while ruinous qualities become manifest."}]}
{"id": "27:25/q18", "question": "Why mention what is concealed before what is declared, and mention both?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:25/q18/p1", "position": "The order echoes the preceding hidden thing and emphasizes God's equal knowledge of secret and public matters.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī gives the thematic echo, says heaven's hidden thing comes first because it fits the context better, and says the manifest is added to broaden the scope or underscore equality. Bursawī likewise says the two terms broaden the scope; al-Biqāʿī notes that even overlapping public utterances are fully known. Al-Ālūsī starts another coordination point, but the surviving excerpt stops before the explanation."}]}
{"id": "27:25/q19", "question": "How does this verse connect to the surrounding account and other scriptural arguments?", "turns_on": "Which feature of the surrounding Solomon and Sheba narrative supplies the connection.", "positions": [{"id": "27:25/q19/p1", "position": "The narrative turns from Sheba's sun worship to a call to worship the God who controls the sun and knows the hidden.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān identifies the transition. Al-Rāzī links God's power and knowledge to refuting sun worship and says the argument's order reverses Abraham's and Moses' because this is specifically about the sun, citing 2:258, 6:76, 26:28 and 27:24. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ likewise infer sole worship from divine creation and knowledge. Ibn Kathīr cites 41:37 against worship of created stars. Islāḥī sees an insertion connecting the ancient scene to Arabia at revelation. Study Quran says the account ends in the queen's acceptance of the One God. Asad reads Satan as immoral impulse evading divine accountability and sun worship as worship of perceptible natural phenomena; he points to Sheba background at 34:15."}, {"id": "27:25/q19/p2", "position": "The hoopoe episode also shows that a humble creature can know what Solomon does not and warns learned people against conceit.", "reasons": "Asad reports al-Rāzī's and al-Zamakhsharī's interpretations of the earlier scene; Abū Ḥayyān notes the hoopoe's claim to know what Solomon did not."}]}
{"id": "27:25/q20", "question": "What report about the hoopoe accompanies this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:25/q20/p1", "position": "The Prophet prohibited killing the hoopoe among four creatures because it called people to worship God alone.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports Abū Hurayra's narration naming the ant, bee, hoopoe and shrike and grades its chain sound."}]}
{"id": "27:25/q21", "question": "What ancillary grammatical analogy is recorded with the light reading?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:25/q21/p1", "position": "The permissibility of omitting a circumstantial element depends on attested usage versus analogy.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports Abū ʿAlī: Sībawayh restricts the omission to attested examples, while al-Akhfash and al-Mubarrad allow it by analogy. The source records this in discussing the lightened construction."}]}
{"id": "28:14/q01", "question": "What does reaching Moses's ashudd denote, and at what age?", "turns_on": "Whether ashudd marks puberty, peak bodily growth, a broad life span, or a fixed reported age; al-Ālūsī questions fixing an age without a reliable report.", "positions": [{"id": "28:14/q01/p1", "position": "Completion or peak of physical strength and growth, without a fixed age.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda and al-Ṭabarī take the expression as vigor; al-Zajjāj says utmost bodily power; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī say growth no longer increases. Biqāʿī includes all capacities. Al-Ālūsī prefers this general sense because timing varies by place, era and circumstance and a precise age needs a reliable report; he questions the inference from 46:15. Ibn Qutayba refers back to an earlier explanation. Abū Isḥāq allows the literal sense of attaining maturity."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p2", "position": "Thirty-three years.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Qatāda and Ibn ʿAbbās are repeatedly cited; al-Thaʿlabī's Ibn ʿAbbās report also says Adam's descendants were allotted sixty years and invokes 35:37. Sources commonly pair thirty-three for ashudd with forty for istiwāʾ; al-Ka

lbī is also reported for thirty-three."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p3", "position": "Puberty or adolescence, approximately fifteen years.", "reasons": "Rabīʿa, Zayd ibn Aslam, Mālik and other exegetes identify the stage with puberty; al-Qurṭubī prefers it, citing the marriage-age test in 4:6. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports roughly fifteen, Muḥammad ibn Qays fifteen, and Iṣlāḥī calls it adolescence, requiring later poise."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p4", "position": "Eighteen years.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Ibn Jubayr give eighteen; another group reports it, and a report from Imam al-Ṣādiq gives eighteen. Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls eighteen the usual age."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p5", "position": "Twenty years.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī, Mujāhid, Yaḥyā ibn Sallām and other reports give twenty."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p6", "position": "Forty years.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and Ibn ʿAbbās and other exegetes identify full strength or full maturity itself with forty, though many other reports apply forty to istiwāʾ."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p7", "position": "Eighteen through thirty years.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī and Ibn ʿAbbās give a bodily-strength span; Ibn ʿAbbās describes a plateau from thirty to forty, then decline. Al-Bayḍāwī associates this span with completed growth and maturing reason."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p9", "position": "Thirty-four years.", "reasons": "Sufyān al-Thawrī supplies thirty-four; al-Qurṭubī presents it as the farthest limit of ashudd."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p10", "position": "Thirty years.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī, an unnamed report and another group give thirty."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p11", "position": "Twenty-five years.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima and another group give twenty-five."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p12", "position": "A few years after thirty, without an exact year.", "reasons": "Attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās; al-Wāḥidī likewise says above thirty."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p13", "position": "Between thirty-three and thirty-nine.", "reasons": "Reported by al-Zajjāj as one view."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p14", "position": "Eighteen through forty.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī attributes this range to Muqātil."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p15", "position": "Fifteen through forty.", "reasons": "Reported by al-Jishumī as one interpretation."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p16", "position": "Eighteen through eighty.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī attributes this unusually broad span to al-Kalbī."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p17", "position": "Sixty-three years.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī attributes this to Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda while also saying istiwāʾ occurred at forty."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p18", "position": "Approximately seventeen through forty.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this from al-Zajjāj."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p19", "position": "Thirty-six years.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes this to a large group."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p20", "position": "The point at which proof and moral responsibility are complete.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan defines the stage by completion of obligation rather than a number."}, {"id": "28:14/q01/p21", "position": "Visible maturity with complete physical and mental strength.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports signs of maturity and both faculties becoming complete."}]}
{"id": "28:14/q02", "question": "What is the grammatical number and singular of ashudd?", "turns_on": "Different analyses take the form as a plural of shidda or shadd, a plural without singular, or a singular noun; authorities' attributions differ.", "positions": [{"id": "28:14/q02/p1", "position": "It is the plural of shidda.", "reasons": "Sībawayh's analysis is reported by al-Naḥḥās and Ibn ʿAṭiyya; al-Jishumī and al-Nasafī compare niʿma/anʿum, while Abū al-Haytham adds the sense of strength and toughness. Al-Māwardī instead attributes shidda to al-Kisāʾī; al-Naḥḥās also lists the alternatives."}, {"id": "28:14/q02/p2", "position": "It is the plural of shadd.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and al-Kisāʾī are cited by Abū ʿUbayda, likening shadd/ashudd to baḥr/abḥur; al-Māwardī assigns this to Sībawayh. Rāzī says al-Farrāʾ treats shadd as analogical but unattested. Attributions vary across sources."}, {"id": "28:14/q02/p3", "position": "It is plural in sense but has no singular of its own form.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda gives this analysis, also transmitted by al-Māwardī. Bursawī describes a singular form built on a plural pattern."}, {"id": "28:14/q02/p4", "position": "It is a singular noun.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and Ibn ʿAṭiyya record this alternative."}, {"id": "28:14/q02/p5", "position": "Ashadd is not the only afʿal singular without tāʾ.", "reasons": "Abū Isḥāq cites the lexicographers' aṣbaʿ; al-Naḥḥās calls denial of this comparison mistaken."}]}
{"id": "28:14/q03", "question": "What does Moses's istiwāʾ denote, and at what age?", "turns_on": "Whether istiwāʾ completes bodily form, intellectual poise, or both, and whether reports fix it at forty or another age.", "positions": [{"id": "28:14/q03/p1", "position": "Mature, settled completion or balance of body and youth, without a fixed age.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda, Ibn Qutayba, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj and al-Zamakhsharī describe settled completion; al-Zamakhsharī cites al-Laqīṭ's poetry. Ibn Shajara emphasizes balanced bodily power; al-Bayḍāwī allows stature or intellect. Al-Ālūsī calls it explanatory of the preceding term.
